I do not think any of the gentlemen who have made remarks this afternoon-some very harsh and very exaggerated remarks-can name a man in the employ of the Intercolonial whom they would appoint to the position of general manager, if they had the power. I shall be glad to get the names if they care to give them.
Will you take the recommendation?
I have to be the judge of that; but I shall be very glad to get the names. The hon. gentleman has not given any name.
I am afraid the minister would not take my recommendation.

Perhaps not. I do not think we should take everybody's recommendation, for after all, as I have said, we are responsible for the running of the road. Complaint has been made about accidents. We have carried seven million passengers this year, the largest number in the history of the road, and we have not killed one passenger-not one. I am willing to leave it to any cpmpetent railway man to judge whether our management has not been an improvement upon any that went before.
With regard to taking off teams, we did not do anything other than what was done on every road in Ontario, by the direction of the Railway 'Commission, in order to help out the transportation question. I am surprised at the statements with regard to trains being late. There is not a train running into Ottawa or Montreal which is not late time and time again. I do not expect that if our Saviour were running the Intercolonial railway He would satisfy a great number of the people down there anyway. I do not expect at all to satisfy them no matter how long I run the road, but I intend to do what I think is right no matter whom it pleases ot whom it does not.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. ^Cochrane) is an interesting psychological study. Hearing the hon. gentleman' this afternoon speaking as he did with apparent candour in reference to the way the Intercolonial has been operated, one would fancy that my hpn. friend was absolutely sincere in the statements he made and actually believed that in the operation of the road he was doing exactly the proper thing. The real fact of the matter is that either my hon. friend is sincere in his assumptions or he is being deceived. We are bound to assume that my hon. friend is sincere in the statements which he has made to the House. If he is sincere he is being grossly deceived in regard to the information that comes to him as to the operation of the Intercolonial. It may be that my hon. friend, psychologically speaking, is not in a position to grasp the theory of the people living along the Intercolonial with regard to the method of

administration. If, as is stated in the country sometimes, it is the intention of this Government to inaugurate a broad system of government ownership of railways, they will have absolutely no supp.ort or sympathy from the people of that part of the Dominion if what they are doing is any indication of what they will do on a larger scale.
My hon. friend suggests that he is under the impression that the Intercolonial is being run satisfactorily. It may be that my hon. friend does not understand the people of the Maritime Provinces. I think that is the real fact of the matter. He does not understand their aspirations, but trusts entirely to subordinates and accepts what they say to him on the supposition that their statements represent the facts. That is the most generous and sympathetic attitude to adopt in regard to my hon. friend. To say that during the last two years there was the slightest appreciation of the conditions that existed in the Maritime Provinces iby the men whp were running the Intercolonial would be to make an absolutely mistaken statement. If one takes a train on that railway at any season of the year, or connects from any of the railways operating in any other part of Canada, one at once sees that the whole system has fallen down. When anything is said they say: The Intercolonial has to haul all the troops that are sailing from Halifax in winter and therefore you should -excuse all these imperfections. But the whole trouble in regard to the management of the Intercolonial in reference to that phase of the situation was that, although this war has lasted for nearly three years, although the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and myself, a year ago, on the 4th of May, said to the then Acting Minister of Railways that the provision at that time in regard to the supply of cars, both for passenger and freight service, was wholly inadequate, and that they ought to have proceeded long before that in order to prepare for the conditions created by the war, it was only at a Hate day that my hon. friend undertook to deal with the question at all. Emfoargos were placed on freight- coming from the Maritime Provinces in 1915 by those who were in control of the railway and the business interests of those provinces suffered in a tremendous degree on account of the lack of foresight of the management. Notwithstanding all that was brought to the attention of the Acting Minister of Railways, totally inadequate provision was made to meet the condition which arose. It was

necessary to have a thousand extra freight oars to deal with that situation in 'an effective way. But, during last winter, the business interests of the Maritime Provinces were tied up again, the whole of the passenger service was dislocated and the conditions, as described toy hon. gentlemen who have spoken before me this afternoon, were not in any degree exaggerated. The 'business men of those provinces could not deal with business men west of Montreal. They were told that the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk refused to give cars to the Intercolonial, because, when they got them down there, they never brought them back. It was impossible to get freight west of Montreal. The same condition existed, by reason of some difference that arose between the management of the Intercolonial and the Canadian Pacific, with reference to the passenger connection at St. John. This was due to a misunderstanding between the men who are operating the Intercolonial and those in charge of connecting roads. Day by day business men came to St. John from the United States or upper Canada to find that the Canadian Pacific train had left half an hour before they arrived, simply because the Intercolonial management would not deal with these roads in what they thought was a proper way.

The freight embargo was put on by the Grand Trunk in Montreal. Under an arrangement, made by the late Government-I do not say it was a bad arrangement-they were unable to handle freight, and therefore we had to bring 49 engines and vans up in order to keep the overseas stuff moving. We could not move freight west simply because the Grand Trunk could net accept it.
What about the Canadian Pacific?
There was an arrangement made by Act of Parliament, but they got the stuff there or at Ste. Rosalie junction.
Not the Canadian Pacific. There is no arrangement by Act of Parliament with the Canadian Pacific.

If a shipper bills
freight from Pictou to Toronto over the Canadian Pacific, we have no right to have it billed by the Grand Trunk.

We were speaking about freight going east, and my hon. friend's remarks apply to freight going west. If my hon. friend had the cars that the
ex-Minister of Railways had pleaded with the acting minister to get in ample quantities, and if he had got the engines that he was asked to get and which he could have got, we would not have had that blockade.
We are not responsible for the blockade. They would not accept a car from us.
You could have taken the cars from them if they would not take the cars from you. All you had to do was to supply engines to take the cars that were tied up at these connecting points.
The Canadian Pacific embargoed stuff going from Montreal. They would not take any freight except for overseas business.

The management of the Intercolonial created these conditions both in regard to passengers and freight, and it is that same kind of management that has caused hon. gentlemen to complain about the conditions to-day. Then, I come to the question, which is the particular subject of this motion, of the promotion of men in the service. The Minister of Customs went off to give us some ancient history in regard to the matter, but my hon. friend did not venture to deal with the proposal, which is the subject of this motion, in regard to promotion of men who are in the service. That is something that is bitterly complained of. It is the thing that caused the former whip of the Conservative party to send his resignation as a member of this House to the chairman of the executive of the party in his county and to resign his position as whip - in this House, and which caused his brother, a member of the Legislature for the county of Colchester, to send his resignation as a member to the Chairman of the Conservative organization in that county; and also, according to his own statement, to decline to take his seat in the Legislature until, as he said, the Minister of Railways came down. Take, for instance, the man who is now Superintendent of the Intercolonial from Saint John to Truro, a man named Devenisih. This man wa's first heard from in connection with railroading as an engineer on the Transcontinental, and it is said that he was very useful to Mr. Gutelius in connection with the preparation of the partisan report which he mads upon the construction of that railway. Let me give an illustration of the extent to which the public are inconvenienced under the

administration of this man. Three weeks ago a through passenger train left St. John on time at two o'clock. At Coid-ibrook it was held up for ten minutes awaiting the arrival of a suburban train running from Rothesay. Imagine a through train withi connections from Boston and New York being held up at a side station for a suburban train on a very short line. Farther along the road they came to Painsee, where they were held up for half an hour waiting to cross another train from the east, when they could have reached Sackville in ten minutes. At McCurdy's siding they were held up to overtake a freight train on a small siding and to wait for another freight train which had left Truro ten minutes before, with the result that the three trains were tied up at this little inconsequential siding three miles out of Truro for nearly an hour. Forty-five passengers going to Prince Edward Island arrived at Truro two hours late by reason of the magnificent superintendence of this gentleman, Mr. Devenish, who was brought to the Intercolonial 'by the minister and Mr. Gute-liua. One passenger said to an official: "This is very queer train dispatching.'' The official said:	"Train dispatching! This is
not train dispatching, this is train detaining." Here is this gentleman, Mr. Devenish, who was not brought up on the Intercolonial, placed in control of that section of the road, without any knowledge of local conditions, and under such circumstances that to-day there is not a 'business man or a patron of the road from Truro to Saint John who does not condemn my hon. friend for having placed that gentleman there. Why was he put there? Does my hon. friend mean to say that there were not men on the Intercolonial, conductors of long experience, men of intelligence and capacity, who were fit to superintend that division of the road? Does he mean to say that there was no man on that railway who could have done that superintending and could not do it to-day better than Mr. Devenish? My hon. friend must recognize these conditions. If he is sincere in the position he takes, for his own good I would advise him to get some information as to exactly what is going on down there. Take, for instance, the case of my hon. friend for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) and his brother. It is all very well for the Minister of Railways to-day to say that he is in favour of the general principle of promotion on the Intercolonial. Why did he, in the year 1915, import twenty-tMr. Macdonald. 1
three men from outside on the Intercolonial? My hon. friend himself gave us the information last winter. On the 26th of April, in answer to the question of my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp), the then Acting-Minister of Railways, told this House that down to Dec. 31, 1915, twenty-three outside men were appointed. In the engineering department there was one man at $500- a month, one at $110 a month, two at $100 a month, one at $165 a month and so on. Some, of these men in different departments were brought in at salaries of from $6,000 to $8,000. In regard to every one of those appointments to positions of a subordinate character under the general manager, there is not a man on the Intercolonial, Liberal or Conservative, who does not know that there are men on the road who could do that work as well as these men. The minister will have to give us in a few days a list of the men he has employed since December, 1915, from outside the Intercolonial, so that we will have this list brought up to date. I presume he will be willing to produce that list. We will then be able to get at the facts in connection with the objections raised by the hon. member for Colchester. My hon. friend says his policy has always been to promote men from the railway staff rather than to take men from outside. That is a remarkable statement in view of the fact that he took on twenty-three outside men, as he said, last year; and I do not know how many he has taken since. I have here what the brother of the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield), who is the member for Colchester in the Provincial House, said. It is just as well that the House should understand, since we are on this question, just what the feeling of the people down there is. Men on the Intercolonial and in the Maritime Provinces are opposed to this Government on account of the way they and the public have been treated. That is the reason why Mr. Stanfield, the member of the local legislature for Colchester, did not take his seat in the House of Assembly. This is what he says:
As you are aware, I did not take my seat in this House until Wednesday last. I represent a county in which a large number of employees of the Canadian Government Railway reside. These employees I consider to be as efficient as any railway men in the world. As a public man, I naturally come into contact with a great many railway men. As a business man, representing large commercial interests, I have constant business dealings with the railway. Questions arose in regard to promotion of employees. I took the ground that the rail-

way management had n >t sufficiently recog-n zed in this respect the merits and the rights of the men. I contended that the principle should he adopted and elearly understood that a 1 promotions to h'gher pcsi ions on the C.G.R. should be given to employees of the said railway.
To emphasize my position in this matter, I deemed it to be advisable to refrain from taking my seat in this House until I obtained assurances in regard to the principle for which I contended.
He does not mention here that in addition to refusing to take his seat in the House he sent his resignation to the Chairman of fhis party, or that he got his brother, the member of this House for the same county, to send his resignation to the Chairman of the Convention in the county and to resign his position as whip of the Conservative party in this House.

Does he say what
pledges he received?

I am coming to that. It is all very well for the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Railways to say that they have recognized in the past the *principle of promotion on the Intercolonial. But if that was so, what was the meaning of the Stanfield brothers acting as they did in this matter of resigning their seats and refusing to continue their positions in the Conservative party, and calling on their party to accept their resignations? Mr. Stanfield goes on:
I am now pleased to be able to make it known to the employees of the Canadian Government Railway system, and to this House, that the management agrees to the general principle of promotion within the ranks, which1 I claimed to be only fair and just.
Wlhat does that mean? That the Minister of Railways had declined to take this position until Mr. Stanfield and his brother had made this threat, and having made the threat they now absolutely say to the people and the Legislature of Nova Scotia that- the Minister of Railways now agrees to the general principle of promotion within t'he ranks, and that he succeeded in this matter. He goes on:
I consider, therefore, that having succeeded in this matter and having, as I believe, vindicated the fair and reasonable rights of the men of the Canadian Government Railway, I am better able to serve their interests and the interests of the public, by being sworn in as a member of this House to which I was elected last June by the votes of the. people of the County of Colchester.
What does that mean? Either that we are to believe the statement of these two members of the Government. to-day that
they have always recognized the principle of promotion, and we are bound to believe them, and that the brothers Stanfield have been, as I have said, in common parlance making a grand stand play for the benefit of their constituents and the railway employees-either that is the situation, or Messrs. Stanfield are telling the truth; that it was necessary for them to threaten to resign their seats and to take the position which one of them in the Legislature of Nova Scotia said it was necessary for him to take before the Government or the Minister of Railways would recognize the principle which is contained in this resolution.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when
the House rose at six o'clock, we were on the point of considering the statement made by Mr Stanfield, the local member for Colchester, in regard to the difference of opinion he had with the Minister of Railways respecting a certain appointment, and I gave the House what Mr. Stanfield had said in the provincial legislature on the subject and pointed out that, as a result of his statement, either the minister was entirely mistaken in the assumption that he has given to the House that in the past he has been in the habit of promoting employees of the Intercolonial to fill the different positions, or Mr. Stanfield is mistaken. This is the statement given by the minister in answer to the questions asked him by the hon. member for Guysboro, as reported in Hansard, page 692:

.	.	. Would the minister he good enough to tell us if he has' rea-lly changed his policy in that regard, and if we may expect that appointments on the eastern division will be made in a different manner in the future?

I have made no change
in policy. My policy is to appoint the best man. If it is possible to find him on the road we certainly take him. It has been my policy ever since I took charge of the department to promote men when I knew they were capable of filling the vacant position.

The minister did not
promise to make any change-is that what we are to understand?
The minister very delicately sidestepped that straight question and answered:

I have said exactly what
I mean.
In other words, he had said what he had said, and he proposed to leave it a mystery

to the speculation of an admiring public as to whether Mr. Stanfield had stampeded him or he had stampeded Mr. Stanfield. I recall that under the regime of the old Empress of China (a regime which has now disappeared, to be superseded by a republic), the admiration of the diplomatic world was always extended to the state documents that were in vogue in those days, because of the marvellous art displayed in all of those documents of what was known in diplomatic circles as "saving their face." It was that marvellous quality which caused the American humorist to say:
For ways that are dark
And tricks that are vain,
The heathen Chinee is peculiar.
Whether it is my hon. friend the minister or the Stanfield family that has resorted to this Oriental system of deceiving the public and throwing dust into their eyes, I a>m not sure, but certainly there was some development of that particular art, because we have these two absolutely distinct statements staring us in the face: on the one hand, the announcement to an admiring public by the self-sacrificing member of the local legislature that he had refrained from taking his seat as a representative of the people in the council halls of the province; that he had sent his resignation to the President of the Conservative Association in the riding by way of protest against the nefarious system which the Minister of Railways had established in the Intercolonial of ignoring the promotion of competent appointees, and on the other, the statement of the minister, reiterated to-day, that he had not in the slightest iota departed from his policy upon that question. These are two absolutely contradictory statements. Were it not for the fact that we have the real facts at our disposal and are able to give them to the House and to the people, members of Parliament would be left in wonderment at the Oriental adeptness of mind of these two gentlemen. The minister 'has the proud satisfaction now of having the former whip of the party state in the House that he was all right again- in somewhat abstruse language, I admit, but still that was the effect. What are the facts? There was the necessity of appointing an official in the city of Halifax to look after the terminals that were being established there. In spite of the pathetic appeals which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) made in the House last year and which my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr Maclean reiterated yes-
terday, pointedly calling the attention of Parliament and the country to the fact that those appeals had fallen on unheeding eaT6, the Minister of Railways continued the old system of patronage on the Intercolonial; and so when this vacancy occurred, along came the Stanfield brothers who recommended to the General Manager or to the minister the appointment of a Mr. McNutt to have charge of those terminals. Mr. McNutt was a train despatcher on the Intercolonial, and a very estimable man as a train despatcher, but I am going to say this to the minister, that when the Stanfields came to him and wanted him to appoint a train de-spatoher to look after the terminals at Halifax, he very properly refused to appoint him, and in that respect he was correct. What did the Stanfields do? They immediately proceeded to declare that the principle of promotion of appointees had been violated by this terrible minister; they set on foot their organ, the Truro Citizen, to belabour the hon. gentleman, which it did in every mood and tense for months to the interest of the people of the Maritime Provinces. The minister, however, foolishly did a wrong thing. Instead of looking around amongst the employees of the Intercolonial and ascertaining whether or not there was a competent conductor or trainman who had experience in handling cars and trains to he found who could be placed in that position, and promoting such a man who would be competent whereas a train despatcher would not be, the minister deserted the Intercolonial altogether, and at the instigation no doubt of his general manager, he proceeded to appoint another man from somewhere else who had no connection with the Intercolonial. The result was that they were both wrong: the Stanfields were wrong because they were recommending a man whose line of training did not fit him for the position-
I never recommended a man.

Well, if my hon.
friend did not recommend him, his brother did. It amounts to the same thing. They proceeded to ask the public to regard them with admiration because they had stood up for the interest of the men on the Intercolonial, while the minister proceeded to have his organs throughout Upper Canada, where the facts were not known, clothe him with a mantle of great virtue and

propriety as standing solidly against this nefarious system of patronage which the hon. member for Colchester was trying to impose upon him. That is the way the game was played.
He was not recommended by a member at all.
Who recommended him?
A railway man, capable of knowing, recommended him.
Recommended whom?
The man my hon. friend is speaking about.
Which man?
The assistant superintendent at Halifax.
The one the minister appointed?
Yes.

I did not say that he was recommended by a member. I said that the minister went to another part of the country to get him. The man recommended by the member for Colchester was Mr. McNutt, a train despatcher of Truro. That was the first act. What was the next? The next act was that Mr. Stanfield, the memher of the provincial tegdslature, proceeded to write a letter to t{ie president of the Conservative Association in his county, who happens to be a brother of the man whom he had recommended for the position. Mr. Stanfield became rather jealous of the adulation which was being extended to the Minister of Railways for having withstood the onslaught of these patronage hunters in Nova Scotia, and he thought he was entitled to some kudos. He immediately started the theory that he was not so particular about McNutt as he was concerning the principle of the promotion of employees and his newspaper sedulously cultivated that idea. Therefore, he sent his resignation to Mr. McNutt the president of the association, and the hon. member for Colchester in this House followed that up by sending in his resignation also. But all the while the minister stands grim and glum behind the great reputation fpr political virtue that he has gathered to himself as the result of standing against the onslaught of the gentleman from Colchester. Then came the third act of the drama. An impasse occurred. The member
for Colchester in the provincial legislature could not take his seat in the face of those conditions. His brother in this House also was troubled as to what his attitude should be. In the interim, after the adjournment of this House had taken place, these two doughty forces which had been battling so sturdily decided to get together. They made a compromise, and the minister created a new job altogether, viz. Inspector of Train Despatchers.
It is not a new job.

How was the
vacancy created?
I forget the gentleman's name who occupied it previously, but he was given another position.
My hon. friend's explanation is worse than his denial.

Like the hon. member
for Peterborough (-Mr. Burnham), he is trying to explain the inexplicable.

drama or not. He is a doughty warrior at long distance. He has threatened the Minister of Railways, and his reputation as a threatener and as a patronage dispenser has extended beyond the bounds of his own province. Whether his appearance to-day with this resolution is for the purpose of enabling these warriors in the play to make their exits gracefully, I am unable to determine. But no matter whether this resolution is agreed to by hon. gentlemen or not, the same old game will go on, notwithstanding the declaration of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and not a man will be employed on the Intercolonial, whether a returned soldier or not, unless he is recommended by the man who has the patronage. That is the situation.
In all frankness I would say to the minister that the complaints which have been made with regard to the operation of the Intercolonial during the last two winters are founded upon absolutely justifiable grounds. We urged last winter, during the absence of the minister, that some prescience, some capacity to look ahead, should be shown by the management. In that marvelous utterance of President Wilson, when he addressed Congress the other day on the duty of the nation in the war, one of the things he laid particular stress upon was the necessity for the transportation companies to use all their efforts, and, by looking ahead, to prepare for the condition which would ensue if war was declared. The obligation which President Wilson sought to impress upon the transportation ^companies of the United States rested equally upon this Government from the very beginning of the war in regard to the Government Railway. The Government knew that it would be necessary to transport our troops and war .materials to the eastern part of Canada over that road, and it was the bounden duty of the management of the Intercolonial the moment war was declared to order such an excess'of equipment over what would be required in normal times, both cars and locomotives, that there would be no danger of holding up the transportation of troops or war material. We asked them in this House to do that, but they never moved. Instead of giving orders to all the car shops in Canada to prepare for the condition which has existed in every one of the 'last three winters, and which will exist again next winter, unless the war should fortunately end before, the Government proceeded to buy some second-hand cars in the United States, with the result

that there have been endless stoppages, tie-ups and vexatious delays, and the common talk in the Maritime Provinces is that it is due wholly and solely to the absolute lack of foresight displayed by the management of the Intercolonial.
My hon. friend said that the General Manager of the Intercolonial was a Canadian citizen. Rightly or wrongly, the people of the Maritime Provinces view the General Manager with some suspicion. It is true he is an American citizen, but the United States is filled with German-American citizens. The General Manager of the Intercolonial came to Canada about 1897, and worked with different railways here until'he was employed as one of the investigating commissioners on the Transcontinental. Although he conducted that inquiry with Senator Staunton, he never took the oath of allegiance to His Majesty King George V, and it was not until after the report had been laid on the table of the House and was under discussion here, and after the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvel!) had asked whether Mr. Gutelius was a Canadian citizen or not, that he proceeded to take the oath of allegiance. One of the men that Mr. Gutelius brought in from outside was a man named Ruhl, who was also said to come from the United States. He was employed at $200 a month as engineer. In the autumn of 1915 there appeared on the eastern portion of the Intercolonial, in the employment of Mr. Ruhl, a man who was unquestionably a German. He had been in Germany until after the war began, and when he came on the Intercolonial he was employed in some out-of-the-way place with some Austrians and Germans. When he came to my town the gang of men with whom he was going to work discovered who he was and refused to work a day longer if he was employed. The man then disappeared. This was in the year 1915. Mr. Ruhl, who had been employed as engineer on the eastern portion of the Intercolonial, went away too, and I do not know whether he is employed on the railway now or not. These are facts about which there is no manner of doubt, and they add to the sense of insecurity and suspicion with which the people of the Maritime Provinces view the management of the Intercolonial.
And when you see everything tied up, as has been the case for the last two or three winters, with trains delayed and lack of connection, and freight impossible to be moved, is it any wonder that there is com-

plaint. This resolution gives us an opportunity to voice the deep feeling that unquestionably exists in the Maritime Provinces with regard to the management of the Intercolonial at 'this time. The minister has told us that he stands where he has always stood with regard to appointments. On the other hand, we have the statement by a prominent public man supporting the minister that he has compelled the minister to recede from the position he formerly held on that question. To-day the minister accepts the motion of his follower from Rimouski (Mr. Boulay), but I am afraid that there will be little result from that resolution and the present debate upon it. The minister will go on enforcing, as he has always done, the principle of patronage ot the fullest degree. He tells us with pride that he has not made dismissals, and says that with regard to dismissals an arrangement exists with the brotherhoods. That arrangement was made by the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), and of course, it must be carried out. But the fact remains that for employees on the road there is a system of demerits, and if an employee is not satisfactory to the person who directs the patronage of the district, every small fault of which he may be guilty will be charged against him in full. I think the minister does not know what goes on in this regard,-I amwbound to say I believe that fully. But the present discussion will enlighten him, and I hope that the result of this discussion and of the acceptance of the resolution will be to enable him to carry into effect that which he says he wishes to carry into effect, due promotion of the men who are employed on the Intercolonial.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) name a man on the Intercolonial whom, if he were the minister, he would appoint as manager?
Mr. MACDONAI\D: I should be glad to confer with my hon. friend and give him a suggestion on that point.
Name one now.
I could name two or three.

This discussion has taken a much wider range than I had expected it would in view of the terms of the resolution. But the minister has told us that he is glad to have suggestions and advice from members of the House or from anybody who has advice to give. I take advantage of the opportunity thus afforded to call his attention to certain matters relating to that portion of the Government Railways system known as the Prince Edward Island Railway. That line has deteriorated very considerably during the last couple of years. The minister smiles-
Yes, I do.
I am satisfied he has had representations made to him about this deterioration.
No.

Let me give the minister some facts within my personal knowledge. The road-bed has deteriorated, because few ties have been supplied within recent years, and many of the ties are rotten, in fact so soft that they will not hold the spikes. The consequence is that trains run off the track. There must be records of these things in the department. I personally have seen the wrecks.
Does the hon. gentleman know of a railway that does not have wrecks?

It is not good management to have ties so rotten and so soft that the rails spread because the spikes do not hold. I myself saw cars that had been wrecked, and their contents destroyed or damaged, the railway being put to a considerable loss. It would be a penny-wise-and-pound-foolish policy to continue this neglect. Again, the rolling stock has deteriorated. I know personally that engines going out to haul trains have not been able to take them to their destination, and other engines have to be sent out to do the work. Many of the engines are leaky. There is a shortage of box cars on the road. Every business man in Prince Edward Island knows that- I do some business in the produce line, and I know that every man who applied for cars last fall had to wait a considerable time before he got them. I should have thought that the minister would have this information, but he does not seem to have it. I understood that the Board of Trade in Charlottetown had made representations to the department on these points, and I presume that the members supporting the Government have also made representations on the same line to the minister. If they have not done so, I think they have been remiss in their duty.
I hope the minister will be able to assure me that this condition of affairs will be improved. If the ties have not been pre-

pared this winter to replace those that have rotted, the minister will have pany wrecks in the fall when the produce is moving. And he will not be able to meet the trade conditions unless more engines and more box cars are provided for the railway. There are capital machine shops in Charlottetown, built several years ago, at which, I should think, a good deal of work could he done. I am confident that the members from Prince Edward Island who support the Government will tell the minister exactly what I have told him. I should be very glad to have his assurance that the conditions will be improved.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
As I am one of those residing in the country served by the Intercolonial railway, I suppose it is in order for me to speak of the management of the road, as we see it in the island of Cape Breton from which I come. If this is to be-regarded as an occasion for imparting information to the minister, then, however great his capacity, I think enough has been given him to make it unnecessary for me to impose further in the same direction. I do not intend to make severe criticism of the management, for I think that, if criticism can produce results in this case, sufficient has already been given to assure us of all we desire. When I read this resolution, I thought it would not cover a criticism of the management, as it relates to promotions to positions as these fall vacant and the men in the service of the road prove fit to fill them.
That phase of the subject was dealt with very fully and satisfactorily by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the necessity of such a policy was so clearly established by him that it would be superfluous on my part to touch upon it any further. I think we must recognize, however, that if there is a management, either by the minister or a board of management, they must take the responsibility of managing the road. While we may suggest .to them the way in which this shall be done, the final responsibility -is with the minister and his officers and the people will hold the minister responsible for the way in which the road is managed. While the Intercolonial, or any other road owned by the Government, is so- held and possessed, no minister need hope to escape criticism. No matter whether there is a general manager, or a board of management, the people of this country through this House will criticise that management 
and the responsible minister must have a seat on the floor of this House and answer to such criticism. Of course, the minister, whether or not he is in fault directly in connection with this mismanagement, if mismanagement there be, must, as a matter of course, take the full responsibility and be answerable to this House.
The minister -and the hon. gentlemen from Quebec, Ontario land farther wes/t hardly -appreciate the situation in Nova Scotia in so far as the Intercolonial is concerned. -Ontario i-s a regular gridiron of railways and if you do not get satisfaction from one road you will get it from another. New Brunswick is in much the same position. In Nova Scotia we have to rely practically on one road. We have the Intercolonial extending through the length of the province from Amherst to Sydney and no other competing road for passengers or freight. It must therefore be understood th-at it is of the highest importance to the public in Nova Scotia that proper management should prevail in connection with that -road. For that reason, we are always bound, in doing our duty to the people we represent, to bring any grievance^ we have to the notice of the minister.
He has had a great many attacks made upon him lately in connection with this matter. My hon. friend f-rom Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has explained the various stages of the very interesting -drama which was played with s.ome degree of manoeuvring between the minister and two hon. gentlemen, one in the local House and the other an honoured and respected member of this House. I have sat in this House for some years since the minister came here, and also before, I have watched his conduct, and no matter what the ho-n. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) may say, I am disposed to. think that the hon. gentleman is in the place in which he was before this row began and that it was up to the hon. member for Colchester to make the most of it and let himself down as gracefully as possible. The play between these hon. gentlemen reminds me of a story that was told me by a little Micmac pupil who was going to school in m>
part of the country. He related to me that one day he had had a falling out with the teacher and I asked him what the trouble was. He said: He always makes me sweep house, draw water, chop wood and put on the fire. One day we made up our minds that we would not

do these things. The teacher said: Why did you not haul the water, why did you not make the fire, why did you not chop the wood, why did you not sweep house? We said: We won't do it. Then, there was an awful row. The little Indian boy was willing to stop there without telling me anything more of the story: I asked:	What
happened, and he replied: We had to draw the water, we had to sweep house, we had to chop the wood, we had to put on the fire, and we all got licked. I believe the minister was the teacher in this case and that the hon. member for Colchester had to haul the water, chop the wood, sweep house, put on the fire and that they all got a licking. No matter how they may tell this to the people of Colchester and of Nova Scotia, I believe that the gentlemen from Colchester climbed down and that the minister is in the same condition that he was in before this row began.
I am sorry that he has found it so very difficult to manage the people of Nova Scotia in connection with this railway. I wish to assure the minister that he would never come across a more kindly people than the people of Cape Breton, a people so easily pleased, or who will appreciate so much anything that is done for them by a-magnate such as the minister. But he tells us that he is going to give up and he suggests that our "saviour" should try to manage the road down there. I am glad that he is generous enough to say that we could get a manager who is not available in the province of Ontario. But I hope he will be able to make another try himself and not put us to the necessity of going out of Ontario looking for suoh a high and sacred management as he suggested this afternoon.
. There are a few things in respect to this management that I would like to bring to the notice of the minister. This is a straight question of management, small in itself, but important to the people of Cape Breton. The minister is aware that under Conservative rule, when the road was built into the island of Cape Breton, about 1890, an hotel was built at the Grand Narrows by a gentleman who then occupied a seat in this House, supporting the Government of the late Sir John A. Macdonald. That hotel was built, and encouraged to be bui'lt, for the accommodation of people travelling on the Intercolonial. It has always been a stopping place for refreshments in the evening on the return of the train arriving at the Grand Narrows about six o'clock. Later on a restaurant was 'built there and
50	I
the public has been accommodated for the last twenty-six or twenty-seven years by the train stopping at this station and allowing the public to patronize these two places. Money has been invested in the hotel and in the restaurant. But, to the consternation of the men who have invested their money in these enterprises, an order was issued preventing the train from stopping at these places, and they have 'been given the go-by. The result of it is that these men are put out of business. That may appear a very small matter to the Government and to the minister, but it is everything to these two men who have put their money into these enterprises, enterprises which have a vested right, having existed in this country for over thirty years. I submit to the minister that by a stroke of the pen he should not put these men out of business in that way. The fact that this hotel and this restaurant were there was a great accommodation to the public. The train stopped for twenty minutes and people were enabled to go to the hotel and the restaurant and get such food as they required. What happens now? You get to the Grand Narrows about six o'clock, and two hours, or two hours and a half, after that you get to Sydney or North Sydney-that is, about eight o'clock-when all the hotels are cleared up and when no food is supplied unless for extraordinary purposes and on extraordinary occasions. The result will be that people will have to go without food; even although they are travelling with small children they must go to bed hungry or else rove around hunting for a restaurant simply because for some freak or other the management of the Intercolonial thought proper to run by this place and not afford the former opportunity of obtaining -food at the customary place. It may be said that passengers can get a meal on the train. A person gets for twenty-five cents or fifty cents all he needs at a restaurant or hotel, but in the dining car he cannot get anything worthy of the name of a meal for less than (fl 50 or $2. People cannot afford that, and the result is that they have to go hungry. The hotel is a splendid hotel, well kept, and a commodious 'building. It is run by a Mr. McNeill, who caters to the public with excellent taste, and is willing on all occasions to do what he can to meet the demands of the public. Those in charge of the restaurant also do what they can to meet the demands of the travelling public. Grand Narrows is one of the beauty spots of the Bras d'Or lakes, and people are always glad to

\

have an opportunity to rest at that hotel. If conditions continue as they have been since January, there will be no hotel, as it could not Ibe kept up without the railway business. This means so much to the travelling public that, as it involves no additional expense to the railway and does not incommode anybody, this request should certainly be granted. The train must stop there for flvie minutes for water and the additonal fifteen minutes would not be missed. I do not wish tn make any harsh criticism of the minister, whom I have always found willing and obliging so far as I am concerned. I must say that so far as railway building in Cape Breton is concerned he has done nothing for us, and I hope that he will not throw any obstacles in the way of further development in railway matters in the island of Cape Breton if the opportunity should come his way. But for the present I am not dealing with that subject. I believe that the minister is just where he was on the management of the Intercolonial. There is no triumph, so far as the member for Colchester is concerned, and I feel that the minister will keep the management himself instead of getting any outside divine aid; and I hope that he will have the trains stop at Grand Narrows as before.

Mr. Speaker, during the few years I have been in this Parliament I have been accustomed year after year to hear members discuss the Intercolonial as though it were a property in which the people of the lower provinces alone were interested. No more fatal misapprehension, it seems to me, could prevail than that. I claim, as one who was born in the lower provinces and who now lives in Western Canada, to have as great an interest, in fact, if not a greater interest in the Intercolonial than the gentlemen who now represent constituencies in the Maritime Provinces. The Intercolonial railway is not in any sense a Maritime Province project only. It is a railway system in the operation of which the whole of Canada is vitally concerned. It is a railway system whose terminals must serve Western Canada if we are to maintain national ports. It is a railway system over which must be carried in winter the major part of the traffic which must give it revenue, -and upon the success of the West and the ability of our people to produce traffic for that road, to no small extent depends not only its prosperity but the future of the great ports of Halifax and St. John. I

regret very greatly to hear gentlemen in this House year after year discuss Intercolonial questions as though they affected individuals only in the counties in which they live.
For a single moment look at the history of that road. It was built as part of the Confederation compact. It was built away from the frontier in order that it might serve a great military purpose, and in order, if occasion necessitated and conditions warranted, that troops might be moved from the East without traversing foreign territory. The wisdom, if you will, of the choice of route has to some extent been vindicated by recent events, and that road, whose construction was part of the Confederation compact or agreement, has, in the largest, the truest and the best sense, served this nation and this Empire since 1914 as has no other piece of track within it.
I should like to remind my friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley)-who, with his usual sophistry, has endeavoured to blame where he should have praised-that no single track in Canada has discharged greater duties, carried more freight and passengers safely, than has the Inter. colonial since the beginning of this war. Let me say that a number of the difficulties under which the Intercolonial is now suffering may be directly traced to observations such as this House has listened to this afternoon. Might I ask my friends, especially my friends from the Maritime Provinces, in the light of the history to which I have referred, to think of the hundreds of millions of dollars of Canadian money that has been poured into that enterprise, conceived as a term of Confederation, and built under very difficult conditions.
Hundreds of millions, does the hon. gentleman say?
Hundreds of millions into the Intercolonial.
Oh, no.
From first to last?
No.
If I had the blue book at hand I could give the figures.
Hundreds of millions is a pretty broad term.
Certainly it is.
I do not think it is correct.

Perhaps the hon. member for Pictou will send across the blue book containing the figures. I have them in my head, but my memory may be inaccurate. That investment is a charge against the people of Canada as a whole, not against the Maritime Provinces. It is an investment upon which interest is being paid by the people of this Dominion, the man in Western Canada as well as the man in Eastern Canada. We must look upon the Intercolonial Railway as a vast national enterprise. It was for that reason that the late Mr. Blair extended it into the city of Montreal. Every one who remembers the conditions under which that road was being operated to Levis will remember the policy upon which hon. gentlemen opposite extended it into Montreal. ' It was that in fact and in deed it might become a national enterprise. This being a national enterprise touching our only two ocean winter ports, St. John and Halifax, we find that from year to year it had a long series of deficits which were charged against the people of Canada as a whole and had to be paid by the taxpayer of British Columbia as well as by the taxpayer of Nova Scotia. Better business management was demanded. When the Railway Act was revised and the Railway Commission created, there was a strong movement on the part of many thoughtful public men in Canada to bring the Intercolonial Railway under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. But, unfortunately, for political reasons, Mr. Blair was not able to do it. Only yesterday I heard the hon. member for St. John City say that he could never quite understand why the Intercolonial and Government roads were not brought under the Commission-and I quite agree. I agree that the time has come when the Intercolonial Railway should be under the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada; when freight and passenger charges should ibe regulated not by political considerations, but by the nature and character of the services rendered. I hope that before the minister has concluded the revision of the Railway Act it will be found possible to bring that road under the Railway 'Commission. The hon.
9 p.m. member for St. John City agreed with that view when he was speaking yesterday in the Railway Committee. I should like as a western man to say this to the House: If we who live upon the plains could enjoy the same freight rates -as you who live along the
50 i
Intercolonial, we would be the most joyous and happy people you ever heard or dreamed of. I wonder if this House realizes that the rates prevailing on the Intercolonial Railway in the province of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island are all the way from 25 to 78 per cent less than those we pay upon the plains for the same services.

They correspond
with the rates generally in fprce in the Maritime Provinces.

They correspond
with the rates in the Maritime Provinces, the hon. gentleman says: But we have it on the authority of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, who has just taken his seat, that there are no other lines there.

As far as the Canadian
Pacific Railway goes.

The Canadian
Pacific Railway dpes not go beyond St. John with its own rails. The lines that are operated in Nova Scotia other than those of the Government have their own rates, because we have not competition within . that territory, as my hon. friend knows. In Prince Edward Island the only line is the Government road.

I have the figures here to which my hon. friend was referring a moment ago. So far from being several hundred millions, the total cost of the Intercolonial railway and connected railways is given on page 88 of the Public Accounts as $106,291,552.
Does that include equipment?

It says: "Intercolonial
and connected railways."
But not equipment.
The amount for canals is $98,000,000. The expenses of canals and the expenses of the Intercolonial railway run pretty nearly together.
The hon. member for St. John city is quite right. He said it was less than $100,000,000; I said over.
You said several hundred millions.
I was wrong in that, because I was including the Transcontinental railway, now being operated as a Government road. Those were the figures I had in mind.
The Transcontinental is a different road altogether.
The figures I had in mind were those applicable to roads now operated by the Government. That is why I may have confused the figures for the moment.
The Transcontinental was so unimportant that it was forgotten.
No, it is such a monument to the incapacity of hon. gentlemen opposite that I did not care to refer to it.
We appreciate the hon. gentleman's consideration.

I thank my hon. friend from St. John for appreciating my consideration, but I do not think the epitaph has yet been wholly written.
Having referred to these deficits and to the efforts of ministers to remedy them, let us look the facts fairly in the eye.
When this Government came into power I happened to know the policy of the present Minister of Railways. Having been born, as I have said, in 'New Brunswick, I took a considerable interest in the Intercolonial railway. It suffered and has suffered from the evil of political patronage, and it will suffer from that evil just so long as it is not under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. There never was a more perfect political machine anywhere than the Intercolonial railway in the time of Hon. Mr. Emmerson. A more perfect political machine could not be conceived, devised and operated than the Intercolonial during the last five years of the fifteen years of Liberal administration. I do not blame them; they were merely improving on conditions as they found them-that is all. I remember discussing the question of the Intercolonial with the Minister of Railways and Canals when the present Administration came into power. He had in his mind two fixed ideas. The first was that the principle of public ownership might be vindicated and the Intercolonial railway saved to the people of Canada. For be it known that the late Minister of Railways and Canals had agreed to hand over the Intercolonial railway to the Canadian Northern interests if the then Government would be sustained in the coming general election. I did not get that second-hand from any one; I have it first hand from the people themselves. The present Minister of Railways did not be-

lieve that the road should be handed over to a private corporation, be it the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern. What he did was to endeavour, with what success I shall presently relate, to bring about such a condition as would vindicate the principle of public ownership of that utility. How did he endeavour to do that? He endeavoured to do it first of all by business management, and, secondly, by the corollary of that, the elimination of patronage. So far as the first point is concerned, what he did was this: he asked the Canadian /Pacific Railway Company for the best railway manager they could give him, and they suggested Mr. Gutelius. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company had had Mr. Gutelius in their employ for many years. The hon. member for Pictou suggested here this evening that he was a German. Mr. Gutelius is a Dutchman by descent and not a German.
I did not say that he was German; I said that he had lived in Canada for fifteen years without having taken out Canadian citizenship.

My hon. friend said
that he was of German extraction; I took the words down at the time.
I said that he was a German-American.

He is not a German-
American, and never was. The ancestors of Mr. Gutelius lived in the United States and have lived upon the American continent for a longer period of years than the ancestors of the distinguished gentleman from Pictou. They have been on this continent something like three hundred years, I am advised. Well, not that long; 250 or thereabouts.
Take another hundred or two off.
He must be Indian.
Fifty feet?

Fifty feet of
snow.
Was that on the level?

That was not on the level. According to hon. gentlemen opposite, one would neveT expect to find anything on the level so far as the Intercolonial is concerned. But the climatic conditions under which that road has to be operated in northern New Brunswick -and Quebec makes it most difficult, and no gentleman knows better than the hon. member for St. John wh-at those difficulties are. The general manager has during the last year been operating his system under exceptional difficulties. First of all, he has had cast upon his line a greater burden than any single line was ever expected to carry. Now that the United States is in the war, our troops and war supplies can be carried by the Canadian Pacific Railway through the state of Maine; prior to that time, however, they could not be, and thus there was thrust upon the Intercolonial a greater burden than any single line ever carried before except some lines west of Lake Superior in the wheat season in the fall of the year. The Intercolonial has discharged that duty fairly well. I have it from the words of an important transportation man in this -country that what has been done by Mr. Gutelius since the outbreak of the war in relation to the management to the Intercolonial has been most commendable, and should merit the commendation of thoughtful Canadians vho know the conditions. It is so easy to criticise. The hon. member for North Cape Breton has been fair about that. As long as the road is operated in the way it is, I suppose it will be criticised, but there is no appreciation on the part of the people of the enormous volume of traffic that road has handled.
The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) spoke this afternoon about the suburban trains being taken off and there not being the same service. I should like to remind him that on the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk, and the Canadian Northern, by order of the Board of Railway Commissioners last fall, their train services were curtailed, because it was necessary in the public interest that it should

be so. If that be so, and Mr. Gutelius has followed that practice on the Intercolonial, who is this high-souled and1 high-minded patriot who has spoken this afternoon in order to make a little political capital? If the 'hon. gentleman seeks to know what is the matter with the Intercolonial, one of the difficulties it suffers from to-day is that there is no . appreciation on the part of members of Parliament and others throughout the territory which it covers of the enormous difficulties it has had to overcome in the matter of handling the business of the country during the last eighteen months. How many hon. members have visited Halifax and seen the freight handled by the Intercolonial there? How many have seen what that road has done in relation to traffic handled since the war broke out? Let them ask the representatives of the British transport system what they think of it.' I prefer their judgment to that of the hon. member for St. John who, for a little cheap clap-trap political capital, has spoken in this House today-and he is not one of those who do not know. He has eyes, but he sees not, and ears but he hears not, lest seeing or hearing he might he converted by the truth. We listened this afternoon to the speech of that hon. gentleman condemning the service and in that calm . way of his talking of wrecks-he did not talk of wars, but of wrecks; he did not talk of the sawdust wharves of by-gone days, but he said there was bad track. It was not the Leary wharf, but bad track. When I hear an hon. gentleman of the years, experience, training, and knowledge of the hon. member for St. John, in a deliberative assembly like the House of Commons of Canada, condemn a railway because there is a wreck, I know that one of two things has happened: either he has a false perspective or he is lacking in the essential elements of patriotism to his country. It is either one of the two things. In this case it is both. With a lack of perspective that is not what I would expect of him in the days that I knew him, he speaks of wrecks as indicating negligence on the part of the Minister of Railways. The Pennsylvania railroad lost in killed and injured 55 passengers the other day, the first they have lost for many years, although they have steel equipment, 90 pound rails and the finest locomotives in the world, because in the last analysis you have to depend upon the human equation, and humanity is frail; it 
may fail in relation to up-keep or to the handling of the locomotive; it may fail in any way. Appliances may fail. Therefore, a man, who, for the sake of cheap political capital, will endeavour to make the people believe, especially in the middle of a great war, that he is speaking in their behalf when he criticises the operations of a railway which has handled hundreds of thousands of his fellow Canadians without the loss of one, and millions of tons of freight for the Allies, is unworthy the name of a Canadian ex-minister of the Crown. He says that the public service has failed. If there has been a lessening of the public service, why should there not be? If the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern are ordered by Sir Henry Drayton to cut down their service, why should the general manager of the Intercolonial not cut down his service. Speaking for my constituents, I voice their .protest with my own when I say that we object to pay unnecessary deficits to keep up the .service on the Intercolonial in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The hon. member is criticising the service because it may influence a small vote in some suburban neighbourhood round about the city of St. John, and the voters may think, how great and glorious is my hon. friend. That is false perspective and false patriotism.
One word more and I shall have concluded. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) was interested in a family quarrel, as he called it. He was more interested in the house of Stanfield than in the house of George, and he was much more interested in the change in the fortunes of the house of Stanfield than he was in the administration of a great public utility. As one hon. gentleman beside me says, he was much more interested in the unshrinkables than in the dye-hards. I do not know just what that means. Now I put it to my hon. friend, who after all is a fair-minded Scotchman-some of my hon. friends doubt whether he is fair-minded, but I can assure them that beneath that somewhat rough exterior there beats a very kindly heart; he can be fair-minded although he does not always show it. I should like to ask my hon. friend from Pictou if he does not believe that the Intercolonial during the last twenty-four months has discharged very great public duties in a manner of which any Canadian might well be proud?

I know a great deal more about the Intercolonial than my hon.

friend does, for he has only travelled over it once or twice, and I would say in all seriousness that the Intercolonial has absolutely failed to perform its national duty in this the greatest crisis in our history.

And the hon.
gentleman beside him (Mr. Pugsley) applauds. It fills him with great glee to think that a public utility operated by this Government is not discharging its duty. He rejoices in it. Let me ask my hon. friend from Pictou what he has done for the Intercolonial? What word of encouragement has he spoken to the men toiling eighteen hours a day to make it successful? What word of	comfort has he
offered to the general manager whom he has vilified and slandered to-night? What effort has he made in the public weal to make the Intercolonial a greater national asset than it has been? That is the question.	What	constructive
suggestions have we heard from him this evening? We have heard a long tirade of criticism and violent denunciation of the nationalities of the men charged with high responsibilities, but we have not heard a word of constructive suggestion; or of help or comfort for those who have toiled in season and out of season to enable the road to carry 300,000 of our fellow-citizens to the sea.

My hon. friend will find that in the session of 1915-1916, standing in my place in Parliament, I called the attention of the railway officials to the extra duty that would be imposed upon them in connection with the war, and pleaded with them to provide in advance the necessary equipment to meet the conditions; but they absolutely failed to do so.

The equipment was ordered. But a single track railway cannot do the impossible, and you cannot doubletrack the Intercolonial railway in war time. But if we had had the rails and the money that have been uselessly sunk between Quebec and Moncton on the National Transcontinental-

Will my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question? Does he deny what I state as a fact, that a very large proportion of the traffic properly belonging to the Intercolonial has been carried over the Transcontinental between Moncton and Quebec?

The hon. gentleman states it as a fact, and his statement of a
fact is always entitled to the consideration it deserves.
The Minister of Railways also knows it to be a fact.
That.will make a difference, but he has not so told me.
Is this a double-track road between those points?
I wish it were a double-track road, because a double-track road means that traffic going in one direction travels on one line, and traffic in the other direction on the other.
That is how the through traffic is operated.
My hon. friend knows much better than I that the operation of the National Transcontinental between Quebec and Moncton has not paid its operating costs.
If my hon. friend will make inquiry he will find that every day during the past year a large number of trains containing fifty, sixty and sometimes seventy oars, pass over the Transcontinental.
The more trains the greater the deficit on that line.
The grade is twice as low as on the Intercolonial.

I thought my hon. friend knew enough about railway matters to know that the greater the number of trains on that section of the Transcontinental the greater the deficit. It is through traffic, and all it gets is its proportion of the through rate, and the through rate has to be so low that the carriage of the traffic over that road means a deficit every time a wheel is turned.

Is my hon. friend not aware that the reason why the Intercolonial authorities have carried such an enormous proportion of the traffic over the Transcontinental is because of its low grades? One locomotive can haul so many more cars than on the Intercolonial.
That is the lowest-grade argument I have heard for a long time. My hon. friend is mistaken.
Will my hon. friend answer my question?
Yes I will, promptly. It is not so.
It is so.

And the hon. member for St. John knows that on that portion of the Transcontinental between Quebec and Moncton the traffic has not paid the operating costs, outside altogether of a single cent of interest on the enormous investment made, and that in the opinion of the best railway experts on the American continent this country would be well served is that there has been no politics in the In-another part of Canada.
Does the hon. gentleman deny that vast quantities of freight have been carried by the Intercolonial authorities of the Transcontinental?
I say this, and I desire to say it as strongly as I can, that to the extent to which that line could be used, it has been used to keep the rails from rusting; that is the position.

The hon. member had
better go over that road once, and he would then change his opinion.
The road travels through territory served by that distinguished servant of the State, the hon. member from 'Carleton, and so it must be a good .one.

I have seen trains on
the Transcontinental pulling seventy-five loaded cars, and as many as ten such trains a day. On the Intercolonial you cannot pull thirty cars with the best engine you have.

I am sorry the
hon. gentleman can count so well on the Transcontinental, and that his vision is s.o obscured on the Intercolonial.

Go over the road and
find out for yourself. You don't know now.

I have seen trains on the Intercolonial with more than thirty or fifty cars. But of course one has a double vision when the traffic is travelling upon one's own pet railway, and a little political capital can be made out of it. The hon. member for Carleton knows as well as any man living, that the r.oad has not justified its existence, in view of the capital expenditure involved in its construction, and never will so far as the present generation is concerned, and that the best masters of American transporation declare not only that the rails should never have been laid, but that they should now be taken up and laid somewhere else where they could be used profitably.

One word about political patronage. As an humble member of the Conservative party ever since the day I was able to think, I go down to the lower provinces occasionally, and the one bitter complaint I have always heard since the year 1911 when the present Government took charge, is that there has been no politics in the intercolonial.
It is the old game on the part of the Liberal party-to charge political administration of the Intercolonial and thus draw a red herring across the trail, while they keep their friends in office on the road. It is so everywhere. It has been so since this war began. They denounce the Tories for putting Tories into office, but when you analyze the facts you will find that the Grits have the jobs, and their friends seek to keep them there by denouncing the Tories for using patronage. It is one of the cleverest schemes of hon. gentlemen opposite. But, on the other hand, you find Tories condemning the management of the Intercolonial for leaving the Liberals in their positions. Down in Moncton and in Westmorland 'how did they vote? Did they vote condemnation of the Government? No. They voted because they were Liberals left over from 1911.

That is not what the
people of Moncton and the railway employees there will tell you. They will tell you that there is no justification for the conduct of the officials of the Intercolonial in the treatment of the men.

The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has raised a second point to Which I wish to refer. The first point was patronage, and the second the low rates. No road in Canada, and with one exception, none on the American continent, has as low freight rates as the Intercolonial. I challenge any hon. gentleman to contravert that statement. Give us in Western Canada the rates that are charged on the Intercolonial and our people will add enormously to their returns. These rates are maintained at the cost of the whole people of Canada, and we have the right to demand efficient administration of the road. But under the devilikh patronage system which grew up prior to 1911, and of which there is no greater disciple than the hon. gentleman from Carleton-
Did the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. B. Bennett) ever hear about the train that was put on between Moncton and Shediac two weeks before the election and was taken off the day after it?

Yes, it was a replacement of a train that used to be there and which had been taken off for efficiency, but the politicians demanded that it should be put back again.
, Mr. CARVELL: Taken off live years ago.

No, only five
months ago, and put back again at the demand of politicians, Tory politicians-and I denounce the Tory politicians for that as much as I do the men whom they feebly imitate.

I thought the hon. gentleman said that there was no patronage, yet !he admits that a train was put on a couple of weeks before an election and then, they having lost the election., it was taken off the day after.

The hon. gentleman did not follow me. I said that the minister endeavoured to conduct the Intercolonial without patronage, but that our own people have not accepted his position but have bitterly complained and criticized him. Yet the principle for which he contended, the principle of Government ownership of that public utility, depends upon a non-political, efficient, business administration. The minister entrusted it to the hands of the general manager, and that general manager, free from political control, might have been able to carry that principle into full effect. But heirs of all the ages though we be, beneficiaries of all the past with regard to the Intercolonial, it was not possible wholly to divorce the administration of the road from politics in a single moment, and the result has been that the minister has been subject to criticism on the part of his own friends. And hon. gentlemen opposite, instead of assisting to maintain and vindicate the principle of public ownership, have taken every opportunity in their power to stimulate criticism and stir the antipathies of the people, in order to make them believe that they are ill-used, although the Government was making a supreme effort to manage this road, not for the people of the Maritime Provinces alone, but for all the people, against the control of a private corporation to which it was to be handed over.
Does that explain the putting on of election trains?

Certainly. Because in the days of the last election, it was not one election train but a whole series of
them, with free tickets handed out by political workers with a view to securing votes. I know this, for I was down there shortly afterwards.
I see that my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has the following notice of motion on the Order Paper:
That, in the opinion of this House, the prevailing system of party patronage constitutes a menace to honest and efficient government, incites to great waste of resources and1 extravagance, in its application to expenditures and' appointments for military purposes, greatly injures the proper fulfilment of our duty to the nation, tends inevitably to corrupt and lower the tone of public morals and should forthwith be eliminated from our Federal administration.
Noble words ! High sentiments ! Lofty aspirations ! But my hon. friend from Pictou and my hon. friend from St. John believe in these things in the abstract. The resolution is put there as a means of throwing dust in the eyes of the people, as the hon. gentleman says the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) has been doing. But if hon. gentlemen opposite were sincere, they would have practiced something of these virtues which they profess in opposition.
I do feel that the members of this House should look upon the Intercolonial railway as something more than two lines of steel owned by the people of the lower provinces. My hon. friend from Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. J. J. Hughes) failed to tell the House, when he talked of lack of equipment, that he was speaking of a narrow-gauge road, one in which standard equipment cannot be used.
We had that information thirty years ago.

I did not know that the hon. gentleman had received it yet, and one would not have supposed that he had it from the way he spoke. I am glad that his constituents had the information thirty years ago, and that he has discovered it to-night. But, in fairness, he should have stated the fact to the House. It is not to be expected that the facilities of a narrow gauge road can be maintained in as high a state of efficiency as those of a standard road. Speaking as one from Western Canada who is interested in the Intercolonial and the work it does, interested in the vast terminals being completed at St. John and Halifax-
Whereabouts at St. John?
Then, when my hon. friend ran an election in 1896 on the cry of better terms for St. John he was merely bluffing because St. John is without all these better facilities yet.
The work is stopped.

The work is stopped in the midst fut the war and I dare say some revenue is stopped a bit also. But it may be that in the midst of war you have to stop some work. That shows the insincerity of my hon. friend when he asks the Government to stop some public undertakings in the midst of the war. If -it should happen that the undertakings are near home it is all bad; if it should happen that they are near some other person's home it is all right. That may be politics but it is not statecraft in the middle of a great war. This House has a right to ask that the Intercolonial shall be so operated, conducted and managed as to sh.ow no deficits but to maintain an equilibrum between revenue and expenditure so that the axiom, or the principle, upon which transportation facilities are provided, may be maintained. What is the principle?-that they who use must pay. With reference to transportation, if the facilities do not pay for themselves in revenue, the rate should be so raised as to enable the revenue to pay the expenditures. The people of the lower provinces objected so strongly a few months ago when the management increased the rates upon the road that the rates had to be reduced again. Under a railway commission that would not happen. I say once more that I have no interest in the Intercolonial except the large interest that every man has who lives in Canada, no interest except to see that it properly serves the great ports of Halifax and St. John. St. John is served, it is true, by the Canadian Pacific, but Halifax is served only by the Intercolonial. I hope, Sir, to see the day when great ships crossing the Atlantic, as the Mauretania did in 90 hours, may be able to land passengers at Halifax at the splendid terminals there, swinging in 'alongside of the dock without tugs, without having to turn the vessel to come in to that magnificent terminal, and being able to embark passengers at the dock head and setting them down in Chicago two days sooner than they could arrive by way of New York.
